🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +0.70% (intraday, 7-year -10bp). At trading day 25 (last close) it was -0.57% against a five-campaign average of -1.46% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.63%. The 10-year is -7bp since the hike vs a +18bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 762bp against a five-year average of 413bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +71bp and BB +45bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.31 → 0.61 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is moving too (+11bp in a month).
  • Bank Earnings: 12 banks reported (CATY, CVBF, FULT, PNFP, SSB, TCBI, WSBC, BPOP, FBP, HBAN, UBSI, VLY); 4 red-flagged (CATY: NCO ratio +45bp QoQ; SSB: NCO ratio +39bp QoQ; WSBC: NPLs +19% QoQ …). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: CATY, SSB, WSBC, VLY.
  • Stocks: Tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 2.6%; the Dow and small caps ended roughly flat.
  • FX: Currencies barely moved; the dollar slipped a touch, yen stayed weak near 157.
  • Technicals: Stocks slipped below their short-term trend but stay above their long-term trend.
  • Sectors: Money left tech and media for staples, utilities, healthcare and banks.
  • Credit/Spreads: Safe corporate bonds look calm, but the riskiest junk bonds are under real strain.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; oil shocks and weak junk borrowers are the hotspots.
  • Inflation: Core price trends are cooling, but energy-driven prices keep the headline sticky.
  • Tech Bubble: Prices aren't near 2000 extremes, but credit is about as complacent as then.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Alphabet is the biggest name reporting; Bloom Energy has the biggest expected swing.
  • Iran: Oil jumped on Hormuz risk; we couldn't verify today's specific Iran headline.
  • Warsh: The Fed meets next week; Warsh gives little guidance, so a hold is our base case.
  • Week Ahead: Fed decision, third-quarter GDP, PCE inflation and megacap tech earnings all land.
  • Outlook: Cautious near term; a defensive tilt makes sense until tech recovers its trend.
  • Trades: Favor defensives over tech, cut the riskiest junk bonds, own short-dated Treasuries.

  • Bottom line: A shift toward safety: oil up, tech down, bonds bid, junk wobbling.

Thursday was a risk-off rotation with a distinct pattern. The S&P 500 fell -1.21% to 7663.43 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped -2.60% to 26008.86. The Dow was flat (+0.02%, 52867.98) and the Russell 2000 edged up +0.11%, so this was a de-rating of growth and tech leadership, not broad liquidation. VIX rose from 16.68 to 19.03 (+14.09%). Abroad the selling was sharper: the Nikkei fell -2.65% and the Euro Stoxx 50 -1.94%. The macro driver looks like a stagflation-tinged energy shock. Brent rose +3.89% to 113.05 and WTI +2.39% to 99.47, while copper (-2.76%) and silver (-5.91%) sold off. Treasuries rallied hard: 2Y -16.6bp to 4.6396% and 10Y -16.6bp to 4.953%, a growth-scare bid rather than an inflation scare. The second story is junk-credit contagion. Headline US HY OAS is a calm 327bp, flat on the day and at the 23rd percentile of history. Underneath, the Bloomberg Caa–B gap is 762bp, the 100th percentile of the past 5 years (5y average 413bp), +231bp in three months and the widest since 2020-04-23. It is no longer just a CCC story. Single-B OAS is +71bp in a month to 316bp, Ba +45bp to 196bp, and IG +11bp to 86bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has jumped to 0.61 from 0.27 a month ago, back near its 5y median of 0.70. So the stress is starting to travel up the ladder, although B and Ba levels are still only around their 5-year median (pctl5y ~51–52). This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Europe is showing the strain first on the day: EUR HY +19bp to 384bp and EUR IG +6bp. Sentiment has moved from complacent to defensive into next week's FOMC (Oct 27–28), Q3 GDP and PCE, and the Alphabet/Microsoft/Amazon earnings cluster.

“When oil runs, tech bleeds and the CCC rot starts climbing into single-B, you don't buy the dip — you buy the bunker.”

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.43 vol points (4th percentile of the 49 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 106.8 (77th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 81bp (steeper by 4bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (121bp above today).

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 21 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — Mixed and leaning toward persistence in the headline, not the core. The trimmed and median core measures are close to target and mostly flat to falling: Median CPI 2.61%, 16% Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.66%, Median PCE 2.57%, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19%, Core Sticky CPI 2.78%. They sit around mid-history percentiles (computed sub-score shown separately). The sticky part comes from energy. Flexible CPI is 6.12% and rising (82nd percentile), Brent is at 113, and Dallas Fed breadth shows 28.9% of the PCE basket inflating above 5% (13.2% above 10%, 15.7% at 5–10%), even as 25.8% of items are falling. Headline Core PCE YoY is 3.01% against Core CPI at 2.6%, and the 1y breakeven of 3.03% sits well above the 5y at 2.39%. Markets see a near-term energy pass-through but anchored longer-run expectations. Wage pressure is not the problem: AHE is 3.0%, ECI is 0.9%, and NFP is just 29k. Our call is energy-driven headline persistence over a cooling core. That complicates Fed cuts but does not argue for hikes unless oil feeds into the sticky basket.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
9 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 59/100
Not a March-2000 replica, but late-cycle in the plumbing. On Equity Froth, today is far from the 2000 peak: Nasdaq trailing P/E 41.25x is 16% of the way to the 175x dot-com extreme, the stretch versus the 200DMA (4.1%) is 8% of the 50% peak, and semis (SOX 37.34x) are 43%. On the Late-cycle Catalyst dimension, credit tightness is beyond 2000 conditions (IG spread 128%, Baa–10Y 165%) and the curve is 69% of the way there. The PMIs show little rollover (9–10%). On Macro Regime, the dollar is at 39% while commodities versus equities reads 200%, because commodities are not cheap relative to stocks, unlike 2000. Among the Bear-Market Signposts, financial conditions (NFCI 154%) and VIX complacency (159%) exceed 2000. Sentiment is not euphoric: AAII bull–bear is -8.9 (27%), consumer confidence 81.9 (17%), margin growth 28.8% (40%) and put/call 75%. Bottom line: valuation and price stretch say no bubble top, but complacent credit and loose financial conditions, now being tested by the CCC widening, are the 2000-style vulnerability.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (41x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The dot-com analogue chart shows the current Nasdaq path (anchored Oct-2022) at 236.7 after 48 months, behind the 1990-anchored dot-com path, which peaked at month 113. That argues the current cycle is earlier and shallower in price terms than 1999–2000. The more relevant 2000 echo is the order of events: credit spreads widened in the low-quality tier first while headline indices held up. Today the Caa–B gap is at a 5-year high while IG and HY headline spreads remain near cycle tights. Our analyst estimates of top-10 S&P concentration (~40%), CAPE (~39x) and market-cap/GDP (~210%) are at or above 2000 levels. That concentration risk is exactly what today's -3.00% tech / -3.02% comm-services day exposed. IPO froth (~30/100) is subdued relative to 2000. Long-term EPS-growth expectations (~65/100) look elevated, with analysts on average seeing S&P 500 Q3 earnings surging over 30%, largely AI-driven (Reuters via Kitco). That is a BofA-style signpost worth watching into next week's megacap reports. All five analyst-estimate inputs are judgment calls and were NOT independently web-verified this run.

⚔️Iran War

We could not verify any Iran-war development dated today (Oct 22) from a major outlet, so we will not attribute Brent's +3.89% move to a specific event. What can be cited: the conflict began in late February/early March 2026 with US and Israeli strikes and Iranian retaliation across Gulf targets (KUOW/NPR). By July 22, CENTCOM reported an 11th straight night of US strikes and Iran claimed drone attacks on US facilities in Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain (Just Security). Later undated AP/CBS headlines describe Trump extending a ceasefire while keeping a blockade on Iranian ports, with uncertainty over peace talks. Windward characterised Hormuz as 'not reopened — in a supervised pause' (via Hellenic Shipping News, undated). Brent traded around $102.60 on Oct 5 (Trading Economics via MoneyMagpie). Today's Bloomberg print of 113.05 therefore implies a meaningful re-escalation premium this month. Goldman has warned Brent stays above $100 through 2026 if a Hormuz closure drags on (Yahoo Finance). Market read: the oil tape is pricing renewed supply risk, but the specific trigger is unverified.

Sources: Early Edition: July 22, 2026 (Just Security) · The latest updates on the Iran war after three weeks (KUOW) · Oil price prediction October 2026 (MoneyMagpie) · Brent to stay above $100 through 2026 if Hormuz closure drags on, warns Goldman Sachs (Yahoo Finance) · Hormuz disruption to keep oil prices firm; $100/bbl risk looms (Hellenic Shipping News)

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

FOMC Oct 27–28 (decision Oct 28, 2pm ET): base case HOLD. This is an inference. Warsh avoids pre-signalling moves, and today's 16.6bp collapse in the 2Y to 4.6396%, cooling core-trend measures and soft payrolls (29k) argue against a hike. Meanwhile Brent at 113.05 and a 3.03% 1y breakeven argue against a cut. Expect little explicit forward guidance.

~1 YEAR

Over ~1 year, our inferred bias is a modestly tighter-than-market stance: a higher bar for cuts while energy keeps headline inflation sticky. Warsh's long-standing preference for a smaller balance sheet suggests continued or accelerated runoff in place of rate cuts. That last point comes from his pre-chair public record and was not re-verified with a source this run.

Verified: Warsh has sharply changed Fed communication, saying less about the economy and inflation, which has frustrated economists and investors (Industrial Distribution). At his late-July press conference he declined to give guidance on hikes, cuts or holds, arguing it limits flexibility and belongs in committee deliberation. Before Jackson Hole (Aug 27–29), futures implied about a 38% chance of a September hike (BeInCrypto/FedWatch). We could not verify what he said at Jackson Hole or what the FOMC did in September, which is a material gap. Our near-term and one-year calls are therefore inference from his communication style plus today's data, not from a fresh on-record statement.

Sources: New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Under Pressure to Clarify Views on Inflation, Interest Rates (Industrial Distribution) · Kevin Warsh Faces First Jackson Hole Test With Markets Split on September Hike (BeInCrypto) · US Economic Calendar October 2026 (fedratecalc)
